name: Fragrance clones (dupes) / Zara
lead: Fragrance clones or "dupes" are inexpensive perfumes designed to smell like well-known designer or niche fragrances. Zara, the Spanish fast-fashion retailer owned by Inditex, sells perfumes and in 2021 launched a beauty line, ZARA Beauty.[3] Online fragrance communities commonly discuss Zara and other budget brands as sources of scents resembling expensive designer releases.

Reverse engineering of best-selling perfumes is described as common in the industry, since gas chromatography equipment is relatively simple to operate and the market is lucrative.[1] Whether a fragrance can be protected by copyright is unsettled: courts in different countries have ruled differently.[1]

paras: Perfume formulas can be analysed with gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, which reveals a general formula, although natural oils complicate the analysis.[1] A related practice, "numbered perfumery" in ex-USSR countries, sells generic-bottled products labelled as an aroma "in the direction of" a known perfume.[1]

Zara is described as a fast-fashion company that brings products to stores far faster than the industry average, and it sells clothing, accessories, beauty products and perfumes.[2] Its encyclopedic entry does not discuss fragrance dupes specifically, though it records fashion-design copying disputes in 2016 and 2018.[2]

It is doubtful that perfumes qualify for US copyright and no US court has ruled on the matter; a scent cannot be trademarked because it is functional.[1] The Dutch Supreme Court granted copyright protection to Lancôme's Trésor in 2006, while the French Supreme Court has twice held that perfumes lack the necessary creativity.[1] Knock-offs sometimes use slightly altered names.[1]

Perfume ingredients are regulated differently by region; the EU requires 26 recognised fragrance allergens to be listed above set thresholds.[1] Fragrance can trigger skin allergy, headaches and asthma reactions in some people.[1] No source reviewed compared clone and original fragrances on safety or longevity.
Fragrance is discussed in appearance and grooming communities as a low-cost way to improve presentation, and dupes are a recurring topic. Specific community sources were not available for citation.

timeline.event: EU rules begin requiring 26 fragrance allergens to be listed.[1]
Dutch Supreme Court grants copyright protection to Lancôme's Trésor.[1]
Zara launches its first beauty line.[2]

card.summary: Cheap lookalike perfumes, with Zara as the best-known retail example; popular for price, with no formal research on how they compare.
card.note: Legal status of copying scents is unsettled; no comparative studies exist.

quick.overview:
Clones or dupes are budget perfumes made to resemble famous designer or niche scents. Zara, a fast-fashion chain, sells perfumes and has been a frequent topic in fragrance communities.

Community members value the price difference; independent comparative research was not found.
quick.mechanism: Producers analyse best-selling perfumes, often with gas chromatography, and formulate similar-smelling blends.
quick.risks: Copyright protection for scents is unsettled and varies by country. As with any perfume, fragrance ingredients can cause skin allergies or asthma reactions in some people.
